## Statement of Need

The mental health of America's young people is in crisis. In 2023, 39.7% of U.S.
high school students reported persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness,
20.4% seriously considered attempting suicide, and 9.5% attempted suicide — rates
that have worsened across nearly every indicator over the past decade. [MH-03]
Yet the care system meant to respond reaches only a fraction of the children who
need it: about half — 49.4% — of the estimated 7.7 million U.S. children with a
treatable mental health disorder do not receive needed treatment from a mental
health professional. [MH-05]

Nebraska feels this gap acutely. About one in four Nebraskans experiences a
behavioral health issue each year, yet provider shortages and long wait times
leave many unable to access care. [MH-01] The state has made real progress —
Nebraska's licensed behavioral health workforce grew 49% from 2010 to 2024, from
2,279 to 3,397 providers, including a 24% increase in rural counties, and
Nebraska remains the only state that tracks its behavioral health workforce
longitudinally. [MH-02] But growth has not closed the gap: demand continues to
outpace supply, and several regions still require families to drive more than an
hour to reach in-person care. A growing workforce in a state this large is
necessary but not sufficient — children still fall through the space between
need and access.

Project Harmony's Connections program exists to close that space: identifying
children who need behavioral health care and navigating them into
evidence-based treatment before crisis becomes catastrophe. The treatment the
program connects children to is not experimental — it is the field's gold
standard. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 61 studies (4,523
participants) found that trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (TF-CBT)
produces large reductions in post-traumatic stress and is superior to control
conditions, establishing it as a first-line treatment for traumatized children.
[E-1] An individual-participant-data meta-analysis published in The Lancet Child
& Adolescent Health confirms trauma-focused CBT as a first-line treatment
irrespective of a child's age, gender, or trauma type — with the greatest
benefit for the most distressed children. [E-2] Investment in Connections funds
the bridge between a child in crisis and a treatment the evidence says works.
